title: Acute stress: under pressure
description: Being put on the spot: timed, judged, expected to perform. The episode follows the first alert, the shift of resources towards vigilance, the hormone response that follows, and the return to balance. Acute stress is an ordinary response that every brain has, not a condition, so there is no "typical response" to compare it with. This is short-lived stress; long-lasting stress is a different matter and is not shown.
caveat: The first step, activity in the insula and the inferior frontal gyrus, is found by two pooled analyses and is the firm part. The rest is less settled. The shift from a control network to a vigilance network and back is a framework its authors propose, built partly on animal work. The hormone step rests on one study, and its finding runs against intuition: in people whose stress hormone rose, the hippocampus, hypothalamus and other regions became less active on the scan, although the hypothalamus is the structure that starts the hormone response. A scan signal going down does not mean every cell in a region is quieter, and the authors propose that the drop is part of how the stress response starts. Scanner stress tasks, such as timed arithmetic with critical feedback, are also a mild stand-in for real pressure.

phases.name: Pressure
phases.caption: The pressure starts: a task against the clock, with someone judging.

phases.name: On alert
phases.caption: The front of the insula and the inferior frontal gyrus become active, the finding the two pooled analyses read here agree on, and the ventral striatum, part of the reward system, becomes less active under social pressure. A proposed framework adds that resources shift towards vigilance and away from control regions; that shift is not drawn because the sources read did not measure it.

order.rationale: The pooled analyses average over whole stress tasks lasting minutes and do not say what comes first. Placing these changes at the start follows the proposed framework in which vigilance rises as soon as stress begins.

phases.name: Hormone response
phases.caption: The stress-hormone system responds. In people whose cortisol rose, one study found the hippocampus, hypothalamus and medial orbitofrontal cortex becoming less active on the scan, the hippocampus most of all in those with the largest hormone rise.

order.rationale: The drop in these regions was measured across the stress task as a whole and related to the hormone rise afterwards. Showing it as a second step, after the first alert, is an inference from the fact that the hormone response is slower than the first reaction.

phases.name: Settling
phases.caption: The pressure is over and activity returns towards rest. A proposed framework says the balance between vigilance and control swings back at this point; that has not been timed in people.

order.rationale: The reversal after stress is part of a proposed framework. No source read for this episode timed it in people.

regions.explanation: The front of the insula is active under stress in two separate pooled analyses. One of them found it for both social pressure and physical stressors such as pain; the other covered social pressure only.

regions.explanation: The starting point of the body's main stress-hormone system. The one human study read here found it less active on the scan in people whose stress hormone rose, which is the opposite of what its role would suggest. It is drawn dimmer, following that measurement; a scan signal going down does not show what the hormone-releasing cells themselves are doing.
